hero.headline: Port St. Lucie residents to receive credits after $24 million settlement with former trash hauler
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will receive money back after the city secured a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro, their former trash hauler. The city and company filed lawsuits against each other in 2021 during the pandemic. The city claimed Waste Pro breached its service standards, while the company blamed a labor shortage caused by the pandemic.

The city voted to return all settlement funds to residents through credits on their property tax bills rather than issuing physical checks. Mayor Shannon Martin said he maintained from the beginning that the funds should benefit residents who experienced problems in 2021 and 2022. Councilman Anthony Bonna said the city reached the sweet spot with the distribution plan. More than 5,700 households with the same owner since 2022 will receive $364, as the city determined they experienced the worst of the service issues, including service interruptions. Councilman David Pickett noted these residents suffered during the litigation process and deserve to be rewarded for that hardship.

Thousands of other homes will receive a $64 credit. This credit accounts for rate increases that occurred during Waste Pro's breach of contract, covering costs for a new waste site, litigation expenses, and the transition to a new provider. Additionally, 24,676 properties that had a title change since 2022 will receive a $64 credit. The city said it cannot determine whether title changes resulted from trusts, marriages, divorces, or relocations, and former owners cannot be reached. New properties numbering 13,241 will also receive the $64 credit because these households also paid the rate increases during the service breach.

Residents who sold a home and purchased another within the city during the same period can submit documentation proving continuous ownership to receive the remaining $300 credit on the following year's tax bill. The city will establish the claims process after staff and the legal department review it. The claims window will last 180 days. A resident named Kelly Lee expressed her satisfaction with the settlement outcome, saying she was pleasantly surprised and that the city presented well thought out plans for distributing the funds fairly among different property owner categories.

cards.headline: Florida property tax amendment officially certified for November ballot
cards.teaser: A proposed constitutional amendment aimed at limiting property tax increases is officially headed to Florida voters in November.
cards.body:
A proposed constitutional amendment aimed at limiting property tax increases is officially headed to Florida voters in November. House Joint Resolution 1-F, titled "Save Our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes," was signed Tuesday by House and Senate officers and filed with Secretary of State Cord Byrd, completing the final procedural step needed to place the measure on the ballot. Because the proposal is a joint resolution rather than a bill, it does not require the Governor's signature. Under Florida law, constitutional amendments can reach the ballot through several avenues, including legislative referral with a three-fifths vote of both chambers.

The measure would require future votes of the electorate before local governments could increase property tax collections beyond certain thresholds. The proposal emerged from this month's Special Session on property tax relief, where lawmakers and the Governor spent weeks negotiating competing visions for what voters should consider. Lawmakers excluded school district property taxes from the amendment, a significant departure from Governor Ron DeSantis's broader push for more sweeping property tax relief. This carveout prompted criticism from the Governor, who signaled disappointment with the final product even as legislative leaders advanced the measure toward the ballot. Constitutional amendments in Florida must receive at least 60 percent voter approval to take effect.

cards.teaser: Jose Arreaga faces five counts of animal cruelty after investigators found dogs in severe states of neglect at a tree farm in the 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway.
cards.body:
Jose Arreaga, 34, identified as the manager of the property at 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway, was arrested Tuesday on a warrant for five counts of animal cruelty. The investigation began June 2 when a community outreach manager contacted the Martin County Sheriff's Office after receiving an anonymous news tip that included photographs allegedly showing deceased dogs on the property.

On June 4, law enforcement found the decomposed remains of a blonde, medium-sized dog in a makeshift enclosure with a tarp roof. Food and water bowls were present but filled with sand, with no evidence they had been used in a significant period of time. Investigators also found a cream-colored male Anatolian shepherd so severely emaciated that he initially appeared to be deceased. This dog struggled to lift his head or move and showed signs of significant pain around his neck. No food or water was found in the area where he was lying. Deputies transported both surviving dogs to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Three puppies were secured over the following day using a trap. All three were Anatolian shepherd/cur mix females presenting with severe flea infestations, open sores across their bodies, and lethargy. The Humane Society's lead veterinarian determined that the emaciated dog's condition was consistent with severe medical neglect, starvation, and malnutrition. Felony animal cruelty charges related to the deceased dog will not be pursued because the advanced state of decomposition made a definitive cause of death unlikely to be established.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach approves nearly $15 million Fern Street railroad crossing to ease downtown traffic
cards.teaser: West Palm Beach commissioners approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street, a move city leaders say will significantly reduce congestion on two of downtown's most overburdened roads.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach commissioners have approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street designed to reduce congestion on two of downtown's most overburdened roads. The project would construct a new at-grade railroad crossing between Tamarind Avenue and Australian Avenue, creating a direct connection between Fern Street and Clearwater Drive. The route is designed to pull traffic away from Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard, which drivers and city officials have identified as choke points in the downtown grid. Fern Street could be widened to five lanes to accommodate expected traffic volume increases. City officials estimate the crossing would divert approximately 10,000 vehicles away from the two congested corridors.

The commission approved Resolution 119-26, a $3 million state-funded grant agreement through the Florida Department of Transportation, and Resolution 120-26F, covering associated funding appropriations. The total estimated cost for the roadway portion is $14.8 million, with remaining funding coming from existing city budget allocations and future sources including HUD grants, mobility fees, and CRA funding. The city is in the preliminary design phase, with the project expected to go out to bid as a design-build contract in fall 2026. Construction is slated to begin in early 2027, with a target completion date of early 2028.

cards.body:
Jose Arreaga, 34, identified as the manager of a tree farm property at 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway, was arrested Tuesday on five counts of animal cruelty, a first-degree misdemeanor. The investigation began June 2 when a community outreach manager contacted Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies after receiving an anonymous news tip that included photographs allegedly showing deceased dogs on the property. On June 4, law enforcement responded and found homemade enclosures matching those in the photographs. Near the residence, investigators discovered a loose reddish-brown, white, and black cur mix female dog identified as Gorda, described as slightly underweight and severely infested with fleas. In one makeshift enclosure, they found the decomposed remains of a blonde, medium-sized dog with what appeared to be a possibly fractured hind leg. Deputies also located a second dog, a cream-colored male Anatolian shepherd, collapsed beneath a tractor and so severely emaciated he initially appeared deceased.

Both dogs were transported to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast and tested positive for heartworm disease. Three puppies, approximately 4 weeks old, were secured using a trap and presented with severe flea infestations, open sores, and lethargy. A brown domestic shorthair cat surrendered by Arreaga gave birth to four stillborn kittens the night of her arrival at the Humane Society. The lead veterinarian determined the male Anatolian shepherd's condition was consistent with severe medical neglect, starvation, and malnutrition. Arreaga was arrested and held at Martin County Jail on $12,500 bond with conditions prohibiting him from owning or maintaining any animals.

While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian, or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit, and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day. Isabel Nylen, a longtime Jupiter resident who has attended several of the dance events, said she understands both sides. Her daughter, Camila Nylen, said Jupiter's beaches are special and residents have a responsibility to protect them. Her daughter, Camila Nylen, emphasized that Jupiter's beaches are special and require careful stewardship. The Town of Jupiter is bringing together all interested stakeholders to work through the controversy. The founder of Happy Beach Dancing declined to comment on the situation. cards.headline: Florida homestead exemption expansion could shift tax burden to renters, critics warn
cards.teaser: A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but critics fear renters may end up paying the price if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue.
cards.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but critics worry renters may face higher costs if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue. A Florida Policy Institute analysis estimates Martin County alone could lose more than $67 million if the amendment passes in November, with statewide losses reaching nearly $4.8 billion. At Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, Executive Director Mike Readling reports an uptick in people seeking help with rent and bills, 95% of whom are renters. "The housing situation is so dire. It's gotten progressively worse," Readling said, adding that the proposed tax cut would do little for the organization's clients.

Attorney John Tolley says local governments facing revenue shortfalls could cut services, dip into reserves, or raise millage rates. If rates rise, homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the exemption, according to realtor Michael Caputo. However, landlords without the exemption could face higher bills and pass costs to renters. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found only 24 affordable rental units available for every 100 extremely low-income renters. The amendment would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10% to 5%. Tolley suggested this could lead to lower rents, while Caputo said the market may stabilize through supply and demand.

Codi Snead announced that the county's first Juneteenth pageant is planned with eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth. The Let's Hear It meetups aim to uncover the real stories that shape communities. Monthly in-person gatherings continue at the library, and residents unable to attend can still participate by emailing LetsHearIt@wptv.com to share concerns and stories.

hero.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties spark debate during sea turtle nesting season
hero.body:
A weekly beach dance gathering in Jupiter has ignited discussion about potential impacts on sea turtle nesting. For three years, Happy Beach Dancing has attracted dozens to hundreds of participants each weekend at beach access 55, drawing people of all ages, families with children, and dogs. Now, some residents are questioning whether the events interfere with turtle nesting during the critical breeding season. Rather than calling for the events to stop entirely, concerned community members are asking organizers to relocate the gatherings during nesting months. Florida beaches are experiencing record numbers of loggerhead and leatherback sea turtle nests this year, making the timing of this debate especially significant.

Jupiter's beaches rank among the world's densest nesting sites for loggerhead sea turtles. According to Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at the Loggerhead Marinelife Center, this small coastal area hosts approximately 150 nests. Walczak explained that the center is not a regulatory body but prioritizes what serves the turtles best. She noted that large crowds gathering on the beach, regardless of their activity, can discourage nesting mother turtles from laying their eggs. This concern forms the core of the ongoing discussion about how the community can balance recreational activities with environmental protection.

Local residents recognize the value of both the dance events and turtle conservation. Isabel Nylen, a longtime Jupiter resident who has attended Happy Beach Dancing, appreciates the inclusive nature of the gatherings and the wide range of participants. However, as a property owner in the area, she also understands the importance of protecting sea turtles and acknowledges the community's commitment to this goal. She pointed to visible efforts like the installation of red lighting on nearby buildings designed to minimize disruption to turtle nesting. Her daughter, Camila Nylen, emphasized that residents bear responsibility for safeguarding Jupiter's special beaches through careful awareness of where they walk and place items.

The Loggerhead Marinelife Center plans to meet with Happy Beach Dancing organizers on Wednesday to discuss potential solutions. The event's founder has declined to comment on the controversy. The Town of Jupiter is convening interested stakeholders to work through this issue collaboratively. The conversation reflects a community working to find common ground between enjoying public spaces and protecting wildlife during a critical time for sea turtle reproduction.

cards.headline: Sargassum seaweed helps and hurts sea turtles on Florida beaches, FAU researchers say
cards.teaser: Florida Atlantic University researchers say sargassum seaweed provides critical habitat for young sea turtles offshore but can become an obstacle for hatchlings when it washes ashore in large amounts.
cards.body:
Emily Turla, laboratory coordinator at Florida Atlantic University's Marine Science Laboratory and a Ph.D. student, explains that sargassum serves as critical habitat for young sea turtles when it remains offshore in ocean currents. After hatching, sea turtle hatchlings swim away from shore, relying on floating mats of sargassum for shelter from predators and food sources during one of the most vulnerable stages of their lives.

Research professor Dr. Brian LaPointe with FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute confirms that sargassum plays an important role in the marine ecosystem. When the seaweed remains in the open ocean, it is deemed essential fish habitat and critical habitat for hatchlings leaving the beach. However, problems arise when excessive amounts of sargassum wash ashore. Large piles of seaweed become obstacles for hatchlings attempting to reach the ocean, sometimes trapping them in the debris. LaPointe notes that the extra time hatchlings spend navigating around the seaweed increases their vulnerability to predators. Researchers say finding ways to manage excessive sargassum while preserving its ecological benefits will continue to be an important challenge for coastal communities as sea turtle nesting season proceeds across South Florida.

cards.headline: Prosecutors to subpoena Tiger Woods medical records after Jupiter Island DUI arrest
cards.teaser: Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island.
cards.body:
Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island. The State of Florida filed a notice on June 15 in the County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit in Martin County, announcing it will issue a subpoena on June 30 for records related to Woods' treatment or hospitalization.

According to the filing, the subpoena will specifically seek any and all reports documenting statements Woods made regarding alcohol or chemical substance use, any and all drug screen results, and the name of the person who performed any testing. The filing was submitted by Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. Any objections to the subpoena must be delivered to the Assistant State Attorney within 10 days.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach ends youth supervision policy
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which had required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. The park said the policy was intermittent and pulled in and out based on work with local authorities and social media trends. It is no longer in effect.

While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day. "At Rapids Water Park, we are committed to providing a safe and family-friendly environment for our guests at all times," Tina Hatcher said in a statement. "We work hand in hand with local officials and monitor social media trends as we uphold strict safety standards through our code of conduct, on-site police officers and a visible security presence." Guests can visit Rapids Water Park's website for additional details before planning their visit.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound mom sets up Little Free Pantry to help neighbors with rising food costs
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound mom is helping neighbors stretch their budgets by setting up a Little Free Pantry right outside her home, aimed at easing the strain of rising food costs.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound mom is helping neighbors stretch their budgets by setting up a Little Free Pantry outside her home to ease the strain of rising food costs. What started as a simple Facebook post to ensure local families could access basic necessities has grown into a steady source of support for anyone in need. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," said Jacquelyn Koester. Located just steps from her home behind the Hobe Sound Public Library, the pantry is stocked with food and baby essentials for families struggling to keep up with higher prices.

Koester says the community response has been overwhelming, with donations regularly filling the shelves after she put out a call for help on Facebook. "When gas prices went up and food prices went up it was just emptying about faster than I can replace it," she said. One anonymous Facebook post from someone who drove up from Jupiter stated, "I drove up from Jupiter for this, this is going to help get me through my week." Koester says those messages keep her motivated to maintain the pantry. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," she said. For more information on how to access the pantry, visit the Facebook group created by Koester.

hero.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach hosts Adults Night and Worlds Largest Swim Lesson
hero.teaser: Rapids Water Park is making waves this summer with a mix of special events aimed at all ages, including glow-filled Adults Night, free admission for dads during Father's Day weekend, and a global safety effort on June 25.
hero.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach is offering special events this summer designed to appeal to visitors of all ages. The park is planning an Adults Night featuring music and glow items, providing exclusive access for guests 21 and older. According to Elliott Russell, the park's director of marketing and sales, the event gives adults an opportunity to experience the slides, lazy river, and wave pool in the evening hours. The park is also recognizing Father's Day by offering free admission for dads on June 20 and 21, allowing families to celebrate together without paying regular ticket prices.

Beyond these recreational offerings, Rapids Water Park is participating in a worldwide initiative focused on water safety. On June 25, the park will join Live Like Jake and numerous other organizations around the globe for the World's Largest Swim Lesson. This coordinated effort aims to raise awareness about water safety and promote swimming instruction on a global scale. By participating in this event, Rapids contributes to a larger mission of educating people about safe practices in and around water.

The park, situated at 6566 N. Military Trail in Riviera Beach, operates daily throughout the season with multiple ticket package options available to suit different budgets and visit lengths. Greg Fuller, the park's general manager, highlighted that the facility continues to enhance the guest experience with new food offerings. This season, specialty funnel cakes and other viral treats are making their debut at the park, giving visitors additional dining options beyond standard amusement park fare.

Whether guests are seeking a fun night out with friends, a family celebration for Father's Day, or an opportunity to learn swimming skills while supporting water safety awareness, Rapids Water Park is positioning itself as a destination offering varied experiences. The combination of evening entertainment for adults, family promotions during holidays, and participation in important safety initiatives demonstrates the park's commitment to serving the Riviera Beach community throughout the summer season.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31 with free activities, incentives and grand prizes.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to "Unearth a Story" this summer as part of its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31. Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen said the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Prizes vary by age group. Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each branch is hosting special events including children's story times, craft sessions, adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character, at various appearances throughout the challenge. According to the American Library Association, summertime reading programs help prevent the "summer slide" in student learning. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

cards.headline: Humane Society thrift stores in Stuart house adoptable cats during shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is temporarily housing adoptable cats at its two thrift stores while undergoing a major renovation of its Palm City shelter. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, shifting many cats to the store locations due to unavailable shelter cages, according to spokesperson Sarah Fisher. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," Fisher said Thursday. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find adoptable cats alongside unique items for sale at both locations. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted, adding that donations of gently used goods are welcome.

The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers rare look at Florida coastal ecosystems
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats through rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman explains that the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex ecosystem models dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, setting it apart from most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said, noting that the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits. The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank recreating one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms including a four-inch barracuda. The touch tank allows guests to handle unusual marine species under staff guidance.

The exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station to raise public awareness about ocean threats while inspiring conservation. Hoffman emphasized that stable ecosystems depend on myriad small organisms, a message reinforced through live displays. The facility, located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, is open year-round. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. More information is available at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

hero.headline: Tampa General Hospital to launch Florida's first newborn genome sequencing program
hero.teaser: Florida is set to become a national example of newborn care this summer with the launch of the Sunshine Genetics Newborn Screening Program at Tampa General Hospital, offering whole genome sequencing to detect serious disease before symptoms appear.
hero.body:
Florida will become a national leader in newborn care this summer when Tampa General Hospital launches the Sunshine Genetics Newborn Screening Program, marking the first statewide effort to offer whole genome sequencing for newborns. The program aims to detect serious genetic diseases before symptoms appear. Established through HB 907, the Sunshine Genetics Act filed in 2025, the legislation was championed by Representative Larry Anderson, whose personal family tragedy drove his determination to create the program. Anderson's son Andrew, known as Drew, was born healthy in 2015 but was diagnosed with Tay-Sachs disease after enduring more than a year of misdiagnoses. Drew died at just 4 years old, prompting Anderson to work toward preventing other families from experiencing the same devastating journey.

The new program represents a significant expansion of Florida's newborn screening capabilities, broadening coverage from 60 conditions to nearly 900 rare genetic diseases. By identifying these conditions early, before symptoms develop, the program could fundamentally change how Florida approaches pediatric care. Anderson announced the legislation before an audience of more than 150 lawmakers, medical students, and patient advocates during Tampa General Hospital's annual advocacy day at the Capitol. "My hope is that families will get the answers that they need, and that babies born today won't have to live that same nightmare of that diagnostic odyssey that I did and that so many families around the country do every day," Anderson said.

The program, developed in partnership with genomic medicine company GeneDx, operates on a voluntary and free basis for participating families. Tampa General will serve as the flagship launch site this summer, with subsequent expansions planned for Orlando and Miami later in the year, leading to a statewide rollout over the next five years. Dr. Patricia Emmanuel, chief of pediatrics at Muma Children's Hospital at TGH, emphasized the program's potential. "It will greatly expand our ability to diagnose these rare conditions," she said. "My hope is that we are able to have a partnership with families to really understand some of the complexities of genetic diseases and to really advance cures. That is our ultimate goal in pediatrics. We want happy, healthy, growing kids."

Supporters of the Sunshine Genetics Newborn Screening Program project significant benefits for Florida's families and healthcare system. Early diagnosis could save the state hundreds of millions of dollars by reducing the lengthy and costly diagnostic process that many rare disease families currently endure. The program also opens pathways to gene therapies and precision treatments that can begin before symptoms appear. The legislature's decision to anchor the program's statewide launch at Tampa General Hospital reflects lawmakers' confidence in the institution's ability to advance innovative care approaches throughout Florida.

cards.headline: Florida property tax amendment officially certified for November ballot
cards.teaser: A proposed constitutional amendment aimed at limiting property tax increases is officially headed to Florida voters in November.
cards.body:
A proposed constitutional amendment aimed at limiting property tax increases is officially headed to Florida voters in November. House Joint Resolution 1-F, titled "Save Our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes," was signed Tuesday by House and Senate officers and filed with Secretary of State Cord Byrd, completing the final procedural step needed to place the measure on the ballot. Because the proposal is a joint resolution rather than a bill, it does not require the Governor's signature. Under Florida law, constitutional amendments can reach the ballot through several avenues, including legislative referral with a three-fifths vote of both chambers.

The measure would require future votes of the electorate before local governments could increase property tax collections beyond certain thresholds. The proposal emerged from this month's Special Session on property tax relief, where lawmakers and the Governor spent weeks negotiating competing visions for what voters should consider. Lawmakers excluded school district property taxes from the amendment, a significant departure from Governor Ron DeSantis's broader push for more sweeping property tax relief. This carveout prompted criticism from the Governor, who signaled disappointment with the final product even as legislative leaders advanced the measure toward the ballot. Constitutional amendments in Florida must receive at least 60 percent voter approval to take effect.

cards.headline: ICE transfers detainees out of 'Alligator Alcatraz' ahead of hurricane season
cards.teaser: Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed that detainees have been moved out of a temporary detention site in Florida commonly referred to as Alligator Alcatraz, citing hurricane preparedness and safety concerns as the state enters peak storm season.
cards.body:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed that detainees have been moved out of a temporary detention site in Florida commonly referred to as "Alligator Alcatraz" ahead of hurricane season. In a statement provided to reporters, ICE said the decision was made to transfer detainees from the soft-sided facility to other locations for their safety as the state enters peak storm season. The agency did not immediately specify how many people were relocated or where they were transferred.

With Atlantic hurricane season underway, authorities said the decision was made to reduce risk to detainees in the event of severe weather impacts. Florida's hurricane season runs from June 1 through November 30, a period when the state frequently faces tropical storms and hurricanes capable of causing widespread flooding, wind damage, and power outages. ICE has not said whether detainees would be returned to the facility after the storm season or if operations at the site would continue in another capacity. State officials have also not publicly outlined any changes to long-term use of the detention site.

cards.headline: Miami-Dade authorizes eminent domain against Fisher Island fuel depot in 11-1 vote
cards.teaser: Miami-Dade County is going to court to seize a fuel yard it passed on buying, with the Commission voting 11-1 to authorize Mayor Daniella Levine Cava to pursue eminent domain against the privately owned fuel depot on Fisher Island that supplies PortMiami.
cards.body:
Miami-Dade County Commission voted 11-1 to authorize Mayor Daniella Levine Cava to pursue eminent domain against a privately owned fuel depot on Fisher Island that supplies PortMiami. The action targets a roughly 10-acre fuel tank farm purchased last year by Chicago-based developer HRP Group for about $180 million. HRP later offered to sell the property to Miami-Dade for $400 million, but Levine Cava and the Commission rejected the price as unreasonable for a depot that has served the port for more than a century. Commissioner Raquel Regalado cast the sole dissenting vote, cautioning that the decision "will impact this county for the next 50 years" and "should not be made lightly."

Commissioner Oliver Gilbert, who is running for Congress, sponsored the resolution. He told reporters the offer was "insane," calling it a more than 100 percent markup for a property flipped in only months. Cruise industry executives from MSC Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line and Royal Caribbean appeared at County Hall supporting the measure as vital to the port's future. Under Florida's eminent domain law, Miami-Dade must observe a 30-day negotiation window before formally filing a petition. Deputy Mayor Roy Coley said the county wants to settle on terms Levine Cava would accept. If negotiations fail, a jury will set the price. HRP stated it intends to contest the taking and blamed the county for "years and decades of failure to plan for PortMiami infrastructure."

cards.headline: State Attorney declines to charge former Citrus County Commissioner in meeting altercation
cards.teaser: Citrus County Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Josh Wooten will not face charges from an altercation with a citizen during a May 12 County Commission meeting, with Fifth Judicial Circuit State Attorney Bill Gladson calling the incident unfortunate but not criminal.
cards.body:
Citrus County Chamber of Commerce President and CEO Josh Wooten will not face charges following an altercation during a May 12 County Commission meeting. Fifth Judicial Circuit State Attorney Bill Gladson issued a "decline to file" memorandum, calling the incident "unfortunate" but not criminal. "While inappropriate and unprofessional, the contact by the suspect in this matter does not rise to the level of criminal prosecution," Gladson wrote. Wooten, a former Citrus County Commissioner, had feuded with board Chair Diana Finegan over how the meeting was being conducted before the incident occurred. He had just concluded remarks regarding the controversial Betz Farm land sale and was returning to his seat when he tapped citizen John Clarke Wray on the shoulder with his rolled-up agenda. Wray immediately jumped up and confronted Wooten, according to a Citrus County Sheriff's Office report.

A commotion can be heard on the meeting audio, with Finegan openly calling for deputies to arrest Wooten for assault. The Sheriff's Office investigated the complaint and sent its findings to the State Attorney for review. Wooten said he was not surprised by Gladson's conclusion, stating that the facts show "there was no ill intent when I briefly tapped the individual's shoulder with papers, after which he rose up and initiated physical contact with me." Wooten said he respects the legal review and considers the matter closed, with his focus remaining on serving the Citrus County business community.

cards.headline: Attorney General Uthmeier leads effort to combat human trafficking during World Cup
cards.teaser: Several law enforcement and business leaders gathered at Florida International University to announce a new effort to reduce human trafficking during the FIFA World Cup, with Attorney General James Uthmeier anchoring the event as the soccer tournament focuses global attention on South Florida.
cards.body:
Several law enforcement and business leaders gathered at Florida International University to announce a new effort to reduce human trafficking during the FIFA World Cup. Attorney General James Uthmeier anchored the event as some 50 business and law enforcement representatives unveiled plans to combat the issue. The games take place at Hard Rock Stadium as well as other major stadiums throughout North America. "It has to be one team to truly tackle this evil," Uthmeier said during the news conference, noting that the World Cup is a dangerous time because many people are coming from other countries where such behavior is more accepted.

Uthmeier announced that Starbucks is donating $1 million to the Florida Alliance to End Human Trafficking, a nonprofit established by the state in 2019. The organization oversees efforts to reduce human trafficking and directs support services for victims recovering from trauma. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones applauded the donation while urging South Florida residents and soccer fans to report suspicious activity during World Cup events. Quiñones challenged observers to contact law enforcement with tips, emphasizing the special phone number to report human trafficking: 305-FIXSTOP.

cards.headline: Erin Peduzzi enters West Palm Beach City Commission race with unanimous City Hall endorsement
cards.teaser: Lawyer, educator and business owner Erin Peduzzi has filed to run for the West Palm Beach City Commission District 4 seat in March 2027, the seat her husband, term-limited Commissioner Joe Peduzzi, will vacate next year.
cards.body:
Lawyer, educator and business owner Erin Peduzzi has filed to run for the West Palm Beach City Commission District 4 seat in March 2027, the seat her term-limited husband Joe Peduzzi will vacate. Erin Peduzzi enters the race with unanimous endorsements from Mayor Keith James and all sitting commissioners: Cathleen Ward (District 1), Shalonda Warren (District 2), Christy Fox (District 3), Steve Sylvester (District 5) and Joe Peduzzi. This gives her the rare distinction of launching a campaign with the entire body she hopes to join already in her corner.

Erin Peduzzi has lived in the city's western communities for nearly two decades. She holds degrees in education and English from Framingham State University, a Master of Education in Curriculum Development from Lesley University, and graduated with honors from Nova Southeastern University's Shepard Broad College of Law, the same law school her husband attended. Before practicing law, she worked as an educator and clinical educator supervising student teachers. Joe Peduzzi, a lawyer who has served since 2019, is in his fourth consecutive and final term, which ends in 2027. He briefly ran for the Palm Beach County Commission District 2 seat before ending that bid last summer.

hero.headline: Florida prosecutors to subpoena Tiger Woods medical records after Jupiter Island DUI arrest
hero.teaser: The State of Florida filed a notice on June 15 announcing it will issue a subpoena on June 30 for records related to Woods' treatment or hospitalization following his March arrest on Jupiter Island.
hero.body:
Prosecutors in Florida are moving forward with obtaining Tiger Woods' medical records as the golfer faces driving under the influence charges stemming from his March arrest on Jupiter Island. Woods pleaded not guilty to the DUI charge, and on June 15, the State of Florida filed notice in Martin County's County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit that it would issue a subpoena on June 30 for records related to any treatment or hospitalization Woods may have received.

The subpoena will focus on specific categories of information from Woods' medical records. Prosecutors are seeking any reports that document statements Woods made about his use of alcohol or chemical substances. Additionally, the state is requesting copies of any drug screening results conducted on Woods and the identification of the person who administered any testing. These records could potentially provide evidence relevant to the DUI case.

Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt filed the notice on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. in the Martin County court. The filing follows standard legal procedures for obtaining medical information in criminal cases. Anyone who wishes to object to the subpoena has a 10-day window from the filing date to submit objections to the Assistant State Attorney's office.

Woods was arrested in March after being found asleep at the wheel on Jupiter Island. The golfer has maintained his not guilty plea despite the charges. The subpoena for his medical records represents a key step in the state's investigation, as prosecutors seek to build their case using documented medical evidence about any substances in Woods' system at the time of his arrest. The medical records could include information about testing performed immediately after his arrest or during any subsequent medical treatment. As the case progresses through the courts in Martin County, both the prosecution and defense will continue to gather evidence and prepare their arguments for what could become a significant legal proceeding.

cards.headline: Martin County man arrested after dead dog, starving dogs found on Connors Highway tree farm
cards.teaser: Jose Arreaga faces five counts of animal cruelty after investigators found dogs in severe states of neglect at a tree farm in the 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway.
cards.body:
Jose Arreaga, 34, identified as the manager of the property at 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway, was arrested Tuesday on a warrant for five counts of animal cruelty. The investigation began June 2 when a community outreach manager contacted the Martin County Sheriff's Office after receiving an anonymous news tip that included photographs allegedly showing deceased dogs on the property.

On June 4, law enforcement found the decomposed remains of a blonde, medium-sized dog in a makeshift enclosure with a tarp roof. Food and water bowls were present but filled with sand, with no evidence they had been used in a significant period of time. Investigators also found a cream-colored male Anatolian shepherd so severely emaciated that he initially appeared to be deceased. This dog struggled to lift his head or move and showed signs of significant pain around his neck. No food or water was found in the area where he was lying. Deputies transported both surviving dogs to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Three puppies were secured over the following day using a trap. All three were Anatolian shepherd/cur mix females presenting with severe flea infestations, open sores across their bodies, and lethargy. The Humane Society's lead veterinarian determined that the emaciated dog's condition was consistent with severe medical neglect, starvation, and malnutrition. Felony animal cruelty charges related to the deceased dog will not be pursued because the advanced state of decomposition made a definitive cause of death unlikely to be established.

cards.headline: Martin County residents push to open high school pool for public swim education
cards.teaser: Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an.
cards.body:
Residents packed a Martin County joint commission meeting on Tuesday, calling on local leaders to open the pool at Martin County High School to the public as an affordable resource for swim education. Patty Beonde spoke about her brother, who drowned at 30 years old after being caught in an undertow. She said he had never been a good swimmer or had real lessons. Ricki Stein, another resident, emphasized that free access is key to getting children comfortable in the water through play. Dick Landrum noted that while several venues in Martin County teach swimming, most charge fees, and he advocated for making the service affordable and community-based.

Those with the nonprofit Martin Swims asked local leaders to put a referendum on the November ballot that would create a fund to establish community pools, suggesting residents pay less than $10 a year per property to fund the pool at Martin County High School. County Commissioner Ed Ciampi said he favors letting the public decide on the importance of swimming education. School District Superintendent Michael Maine said he is already planning to meet with Martin Swims to explore logistics and determine what the school district can feasibly do. Dr. Blanche Wells, president of Martin Swims, said the cause is personal and urgent, stating that as lifelong swimmers they are devoted to the effort because it is life-saving.

cards.headline: Republican lawmakers tour Lake Okeechobee to discuss water quality and restoration efforts
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers from across Florida toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday, discussing ongoing and future efforts to revitalize the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians.
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss restoration efforts for the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians. Rep. Toby Overdorf of Martin County and Meg Weinberger, who represents western Palm Beach County, joined Congressman and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds on the tour. Overdorf said the area faces nutrient issues, vegetation problems, and management challenges that converge at the lake. Donalds emphasized completing long-planned restoration projects, including a potential reservoir north of the lake on the Kissimmee River Basin to manage water levels. He also identified sediment removal from the lake bottom as a key priority going forward.

Friends of the Everglades acknowledged the value of the tour but argued the next governor should prioritize water storage and treatment projects south of Lake Okeechobee instead. Executive Director Eve Samples noted that Lake Okeechobee is one of the most polluted lakes in North America and that the Southern Everglades are on track to fail phosphorus pollution limits with deadlines this year. Samples said investing in storage and treatment south of the lake would deliver greater returns for taxpayer dollars, as cleaned water could be sent to the Southern Everglades, which currently does not receive enough fresh clean water.

cards.headline: Weekend beach dance parties in Jupiter spark debate over sea turtle nesting season
cards.teaser: A popular weekend beach dance party at beach access 55 in Jupiter is at the center of a debate over whether the gatherings are disrupting sea turtle nests during nesting season.
cards.body:
For the past three years, dozens and sometimes hundreds of people have gathered at beach access 55 in Jupiter for an event called "Happy Beach Dancing." The weekly meetup has drawn people of all ages, families, children, and dogs. Some residents are concerned the gatherings disrupt sea turtle nests, though the movement is not to shut the event down but to ask the dancers to relocate during nesting season.

Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at the nearby Loggerhead Marinelife Center, said Jupiter's beaches are among the densest nesting sites for loggerheads in the entire world, with 150 nests in this small area. She said the center is not a regulatory agency and their focus is on doing what is best for the turtles. "Just the fact that a large crowd gathered on the beach, no matter what they're doing, can deter the mama turtles from doing their nesting," Walczak said. The Loggerhead Marinelife Center plans to meet with the dance party organizers on Wednesday to discuss the issue. The Town of Jupiter is gathering all interested stakeholders for this conversation.

cards.headline: Sargassum seaweed helps and hurts Florida sea turtles during nesting season
cards.teaser: Researchers say sargassum provides critical habitat for young sea turtles offshore, but excessive amounts washing ashore can create obstacles for hatchlings trying to reach the ocean.
cards.body:
For many Florida beachgoers, sargassum is a nuisance that piles up along shorelines, creating unpleasant odors and making beach walks less enjoyable. But researchers say the brown seaweed's relationship with sea turtles is far more complicated. "Sargassum is an important habitat for young sea turtles when it's out offshore in the currents because that's where they swim out to right as they get off the beach," said Emily Turla, laboratory coordinator at Florida Atlantic University's Marine Science Laboratory and a Ph.D. student. After hatching, young sea turtles spend their first days swimming away from shore, and floating mats of sargassum provide shelter from predators, food sources, and critical habitat during one of the most vulnerable stages of their lives.

The problem emerges when excessive amounts of sargassum wash ashore. Scientists say large piles of seaweed become obstacles for hatchlings trying to reach the ocean. "Sometimes you'll be walking along the beach and see them kind of stuck in it," Turla said. Research professor Dr. Brian LaPointe with FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute explains that the extra time hatchlings spend navigating around seaweed increases their vulnerability to predators. Researchers say finding ways to manage excessive sargassum while preserving its ecological benefits will remain an important challenge for coastal communities as sea turtle nesting season continues across South Florida.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach approves nearly $15 million Fern Street railroad crossing to ease downtown traffic
cards.teaser: West Palm Beach commissioners approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street between Tamarind Avenue and Australian Avenue, designed to pull traffic away from Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach commissioners have approved a nearly $15 million project to build a new railroad crossing on Fern Street designed to reduce congestion on two of downtown's most overburdened roads. The Fern Street railroad project would construct a new at-grade railroad crossing between Tamarind Avenue and Australian Avenue, creating a direct connection between Fern Street and Clearwater Drive. The route is designed to pull traffic away from Okeechobee Boulevard and Banyan Boulevard, which drivers and city officials alike have long identified as choke points in the downtown grid. Fern Street itself could be widened to five lanes to accommodate the expected increase in traffic volume. City officials estimate the crossing would divert approximately 10,000 vehicles away from the two congested corridors.

The commission approved two resolutions at its meeting: Resolution 119-26, a $3 million state-funded grant agreement through the Florida Department of Transportation, and Resolution 120-26F, covering associated funding appropriations. The total estimated cost for the roadway portion is $14.8 million. The remainder of the funding would come from existing city budget allocations and future sources including HUD grants, mobility fees, and CRA funding. The city is currently in the preliminary design phase. The project is expected to go out to bid as a design-build contract in fall 2026, with construction slated to begin in early 2027 and a target completion date of early 2028.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents to receive tax credits after $24 million Waste Pro settlement
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will receive credits on their property tax bills after the city received a $24 million settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro. The city council voted to return all settlement funds to residents through tax credits rather than physical checks. The city and Waste Pro filed lawsuits against each other in 2021 during the pandemic. The city claimed Waste Pro breached its contract for its standard of service, while the company blamed a pandemic labor shortage. Mayor Shannon Martin said the funds should benefit residents who experienced the issues in 2021 and 2022. Councilman Anthony Bonna said the city has reached the sweet spot with the distribution plan.

More than 5,700 households with the same owner since 2022 will receive $364 because the city says they received the brunt of service interruptions during Waste Pro's breach of contract. Thousands of other homes will receive a $64 credit due to rate increases during the breach, including costs for a new waste site, litigation costs and moving to a new provider. The city said 24,676 properties had a title change since 2022 and 13,241 new properties were built, all receiving the $64 credit. Residents who sold a home and purchased another within the city during the same period may submit documentation showing continuous ownership to receive the remaining $300 credit on the following year's tax bill through a 180-day claims window.

hero.headline: Tiger Woods medical records to be subpoenaed in Jupiter Island DUI case
hero.teaser: Florida prosecutors will issue a subpoena for Tiger Woods' medical records after he pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence following an arrest in March on Jupiter Island.
hero.body:
Florida prosecutors have announced plans to obtain Tiger Woods' medical records as part of the ongoing investigation into his driving under the influence arrest. Woods pleaded not guilty to the DUI charge following his arrest in March on Jupiter Island. On June 15, the State of Florida filed a notice in the County Court of the Nineteenth Judicial Circuit in Martin County indicating that a subpoena would be issued on June 30 to obtain records related to Woods' treatment or hospitalization.

The subpoena will seek specific types of information from Woods' medical providers. Prosecutors are looking for any reports that document statements Woods made about his use of alcohol or chemical substances. The subpoena will also require the production of all drug screen results related to Woods' medical treatment or evaluation. Additionally, prosecutors want to identify the name of any person who performed testing on Woods during his treatment or hospitalization.

Assistant State Attorney Nirlaine Tallandier Smartt filed the notice on behalf of State Attorney Thomas R. The filing gives interested parties a window to object to the subpoena. Anyone with objections to the request for medical records has 10 days from the filing date to deliver their objections to the Assistant State Attorney's office.

This move represents a standard prosecutorial step in DUI cases, where medical records can provide relevant information about a defendant's condition at the time of arrest. The subpoena specifically targets documentation of Woods' own statements about substance use and any test results that could be relevant to the DUI charges. The case will continue to develop through the court system as both the prosecution and defense prepare their arguments.

cards.headline: Property owner arrested after dead dog, starving animals found at Martin County tree farm
cards.teaser: Jose Arreaga, 34, the manager of a property in the 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway, was arrested Tuesday on five counts of animal cruelty after Martin .
cards.body:
Jose Arreaga, 34, identified as the manager of a property in the 16000 block of Southwest Connors Highway, was arrested Tuesday on five counts of animal cruelty, a first-degree misdemeanor. The investigation began June 2 when a community outreach manager contacted Martin County Sheriff's deputies after receiving an anonymous tip with photographs allegedly showing deceased dogs on the property. Deputies responded June 4 and found a decomposed dog in a makeshift enclosure with food and water bowls filled with sand and no evidence of recent use. They also discovered a cream-colored male Anatolian shepherd collapsed beneath a tractor, so severely emaciated he initially appeared dead. The dog, weighing significantly less than the typical 120 pounds for a male Anatolian shepherd, had to be carried into the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. A reddish-brown, white, and black cur mix female dog named Gorda was found severely infested with fleas and heavily lactating.

Over the following day, three puppies approximately 4 weeks old were trapped and secured. All three presented with severe flea infestations, open sores, and lethargy requiring multiple baths at the Humane Society. A brown domestic shorthair cat surrendered by Arreaga gave birth the night of her arrival, with all four kittens stillborn. The Humane Society's lead veterinarian determined the emaciated dog's condition was consistent with severe medical neglect, starvation, and malnutrition. Both Gorda and the male Anatolian shepherd tested positive for heartworm disease. All three puppies were diagnosed with severe ringworm, flea bite dermatitis, fungal infection, bacterial skin conditions, hookworms, and severe flea infestation causing anemia. Arreaga was taken to Martin County Jail on $12,500 bond with conditions prohibiting him from owning or maintaining animals.

cards.headline: Jupiter beach dance parties spark debate during sea turtle nesting season
cards.teaser: Dozens and sometimes hundreds of people have gathered at beach access 55 in Jupiter for an event called Happy Beach Dancing for the past three years, but some residents are concerned the gatherings disrupt sea turtle nests.
cards.body:
Isabel Nylen, a longtime Jupiter resident who has attended several of the dance events, said people of all ages come with families, little kids, and dogs. Her daughter Camila Nylen said Jupiter's beaches are special and that residents have a responsibility to protect them, requiring care about where items are placed and where people walk. The movement is not to shut down the weekly "Happy Beach Dancing" event at beach access 55, but to ask the dancers to relocate during nesting season.

Joanna Walczak, Vice President of Conservation at the nearby Loggerhead Marinelife Center, said Jupiter's beaches are among the densest nesting sites for loggerheads in the entire world, with 150 nests in this small area. She said that just a large crowd gathered on the beach, no matter the activity, can deter mama turtles from nesting. The Loggerhead Marinelife Center plans to meet with the dance party organizers on Wednesday to discuss the issue. The Town of Jupiter is gathering all interested stakeholders for this conversation.

cards.teaser: Sargassum seaweed provides essential habitat for young sea turtles offshore, but can become an obstacle for hatchlings when it washes ashore in large amounts.

Research professor Dr. Brian LaPointe with FAU's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute noted that when sargassum is in the open ocean, it is deemed essential fish habitat and critical habitat for hatchlings leaving the beach.

cards.headline: Republican lawmakers tour Lake Okeechobee to discuss water quality and restoration
cards.teaser: Republican lawmakers from across Florida toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday, discussing ongoing and future efforts to revitalize the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians.
cards.body:
Republican lawmakers toured Lake Okeechobee by airboat Tuesday to discuss restoration efforts for the waterway that provides drinking water to more than 6 million South Floridians. Rep. Toby Overdorf of Martin County said the lake is foundational to the region's water systems. "This is an area that then everything else flows from. We have nutrient issues, we have overall vegetation issues, with management issues, and all of these things are coming together at this one particular area," Overdorf said. Meg Weinberger, who represents western Palm Beach County, emphasized the importance of educating residents about the lake. "This is the most important. If you're living in Florida, we need to learn, we need to teach our kids, and many Floridians really have no clue what goes on in Lake Okeechobee," Weinberger said.

Congressman and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds highlighted completion of planned restoration projects, including a potential reservoir north of the lake on the Kissimmee River Basin to manage water levels. However, Friends of the Everglades Executive Director Eve Samples argued for a different priority. She noted that Lake Okeechobee is one of the most polluted lakes in North America and that the Southern Everglades face phosphorus pollution limits with deadlines kicking in this year. Samples said "the greatest bang for Floridians' bucks" would be water storage and treatment projects south of Lake Okeechobee rather than north of it.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach ends interim youth supervision policy
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which had required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has ended its interim youth supervision policy, which required guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. The park said the policy is intermittent and pulled in and out based on work with local authorities and social media trends. It is no longer in effect.

While in effect, the policy required minors ages 17 and under to be accompanied by a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who was at least 21 years old and had traveled to the park with the minor's group. Adult chaperones were required to present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry, remain on-site for the duration of the visit and were limited to supervising no more than five guests ages 17 and under per day. According to Tina Hatcher, the park is committed to providing a safe and family-friendly environment by working hand in hand with local officials, monitoring social media trends and upholding strict safety standards through its code of conduct, on-site police officers and visible security presence.
